title: Question 9
stem: Fluorine-18 ($^{18}_{9}\text{F}$) decays by beta-plus ($\beta^{+}$) emission with a half-life of 110 minutes.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State the name of the beta-plus particle.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the symbols $\beta^-$ and $\beta^+$ - if $\beta^-$ is an electron, what is the antimatter equivalent with the same mass but opposite charge?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what beta particles are**
You already know $\beta^-$ radiation is fast-moving electrons emitted from the nucleus. $\beta^+$ is the positive version.

Step 2: **Name the antimatter electron**
The particle with the same mass as an electron but with $+e$ charge is called the positron. So the $\beta^+$ particle is a positron.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Show that the decay constant of fluorine-18 is $1.05 \times 10^{-4} \text{s}^{-1}$.
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about the units needed - the decay constant must be in $\text{s}^{-1}$, so what must you first do to the half-life of 110 minutes?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link half-life to decay constant**
Half-life $T_{1/2}$ is the time for half the nuclei to decay. A larger decay constant $\lambda$ means faster decay. They are linked by $$\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$$ where $T_{1/2}$ must be in seconds to give $\lambda$ in $\text{s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Convert and calculate**
Convert 110 minutes to seconds: $$T_{1/2} = 110 \times 60 = 6600 \text{ s}$$ Then $$\lambda = \frac{0.693}{6600} = 1.05 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1}$$ This is the value to be shown.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: Determine the activity of $2.1 \times 10^{-12}\text{kg}$ of fluorine-18.
hints: Hint 1: Activity tells you how many decays per second, so it must depend on two things - how fast each nucleus is likely to decay and how many nuclei you have. Which of these do you already know?

Hint 2: To find the number of nuclei $N$, compare the total sample mass to the mass of one fluorine-18 nucleus - remember mass number 18 means about $18\text{ u}$ per nucleus where $1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$.
Hint 3: Now combine your $N$ with the decay constant from (a)(ii) using $A = \lambda N$ and check your power of ten and unit of $\text{Bq}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the number of undecayed nuclei N**
Activity needs $N$. Each $^{18}\text{F}$ nucleus has mass approx $18\text{ u}$: $$m_{atom} = 18 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg} = 2.99 \times 10^{-26} \text{ kg}$$ Divide total mass by mass per nucleus: $$N = \frac{2.1 \times 10^{-12}}{18 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 7.0 \times 10^{13}$$

Step 2: **Apply the activity equation**
Activity is the rate of decay: $$A = \lambda N$$ This makes sense - double the nuclei or double the probability per second and you double the decays per second.

Step 3: **Calculate the activity**
Use $\lambda = 1.05 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1}$: $$A = 1.05 \times 10^{-4} \times 7.0 \times 10^{13} = 7.4 \times 10^{9} \text{ Bq}$$ where $1 \text{ Bq} = 1$ decay per second.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: A small sample of fluorine-18 injected into the body acts as a tracer for use in medical imaging.
parts.text: Describe how the interaction of a $\beta^{+}$ particle with an electron in the body enables the formation of an image.

markscheme_points.text: (pair) annihilation occurs; the mass of the two particles is converted into energy; two gamma photons are formed and travel in opposite directions or two gamma photons are formed and leave the body; difference in arrival times of photons (at detector) is processed; Any three points, 1 mark each

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens when matter meets antimatter - a $\beta^+$ positron meeting an ordinary electron in tissue cannot just bounce off, so what must happen to their mass?
Hint 2: Recall conservation of momentum - if the positron and electron are almost at rest when they meet, why must two gamma photons be emitted in opposite directions rather than just one?
Hint 3: For imaging, how could detectors around the body use the arrival of these photons to work out where in the body the decay happened?
parts.proper_answer: Positron and electron undergo pair annihilation, mass converted to energy as two gamma photons emitted in opposite directions. Photons detected outside body and timing / position processed by computer to locate emission point and build image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pair annihilation**
The emitted positron slows down and meets an electron in the body. Particle and antiparticle annihilate each other. Their total mass disappears and is converted into electromagnetic energy, as $E = mc^2$.

Step 2: **Two gamma photons in opposite directions**
Energy and momentum must be conserved, so two gamma-ray photons are created travelling in exactly opposite directions (180 degrees apart) along the same line.

Step 3: **Detection to form an image**
The gamma photons escape the body and are detected by a ring of detectors. Where the tracer is concentrated, more annihilations occur. A computer uses the positions and small difference in arrival times of each photon pair to locate the annihilation point, building up a map of tracer concentration which is the image.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Suggest why 110 minutes is a suitable half-life for a nuclide used as a tracer in medical diagnosis.

markscheme_points.text: with a shorter half-life: sample would (almost) fully decay before the test is complete
a longer half-life: exposes patient to harmful/ionising radiation unnecessarily or with a longer half-life: a larger dose (of tracer) needed to produce detectable activity

hints: Hint 1: Imagine the half-life was only a few seconds - what would happen to the tracer between injection and taking the image a while later?

Hint 2: Now imagine the opposite extreme - a half-life of many years. Why would the patient keep receiving ionising radiation long after the scan, or why would you need a much larger initial amount to get a clear signal?
parts.proper_answer: Shorter half-life would decay away before diagnosis complete, giving too little activity to detect. Longer half-life would give unnecessary prolonged ionising radiation dose to patient / require larger dose for same detectable activity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why not much shorter**
If the half-life were much shorter than 110 minutes, the sample would almost fully decay before the tracer has circulated and the scan is finished. Activity would fall too fast to get a useful image.

Step 2: **Why not much longer**
If the half-life were much longer, the nuclei decay very slowly, so activity per mass is low. You would need a larger mass of tracer to get enough signal, and the patient would remain radioactive long after the test, receiving harmful ionising radiation unnecessarily. 110 minutes is long enough for the scan but short enough to decay away quickly afterwards.
